summary: Green hydrogen technicians operate and maintain the electrolyzers, water treatment, compression and storage systems at plants that make hydrogen from renewable power, working for developers, utilities, refiners, electrolyzer OEMs and hydrogen hub projects. Claude helps most with reading stack performance trends, drafting procedures and shift reports, working through codes like NFPA 2 and ISO 22734, and documenting the operating data that 'green' certification schemes like the EU RFNBO rules and US 45V depend on.

prompts.title: Stack degradation trend review
prompts.task: Spot abnormal electrolyzer stack degradation from operating data
prompts.prompt: You are an experienced electrolyzer performance engineer. I'm a technician at a [PEM / alkaline / solid oxide] plant running [NUMBER] stacks from [OEM, if allowed to share]. Below is [TIME PERIOD] of data per stack: cell or stack voltage at reference current density, current density, stack temperature, pressure, water conductivity, and hours run. [PASTE DATA OR SUMMARY]. The OEM's expected degradation rate is [VALUE, e.g. µV/h per cell]. Please: (1) work out each stack's degradation rate and flag any above expectation; (2) list likely causes for each flagged stack (e.g. feed water contamination, membrane thinning, catalyst loss, frequent cycling from variable renewable power), ranked by how well the data fits; (3) suggest which extra measurements would tell those causes apart. Present it as a table followed by short notes. Where the data can't support a conclusion, say so.
prompts.caution: Trend analysis only; follow the OEM's diagnostic procedures and warranty terms before any intervention on a stack.

prompts.title: Hydrogen leak alarm troubleshooting
prompts.task: Structured fault-finding after a gas detector or H2-in-O2 alarm
prompts.prompt: Act as a senior hydrogen plant commissioning engineer. During [OPERATING STATE, e.g. ramp-up after a curtailment] our [PEM/alkaline] electrolyzer tripped on [ALARM: e.g. H2-in-O2 above X% LEL, area gas detector, low stack differential pressure]. The plant is now in [CURRENT SAFE STATE]. Here are the alarm and event logs and relevant trends: [PASTE]. Build a fault tree for this trip covering instrument faults, process causes (e.g. membrane crossover, separator level, purge failure) and leaks. For each branch, give the evidence that supports or rules it out from the logs, the check I could do and its hazard class, and whether it needs a permit, LOTO or gas-free certification. Stop at checks only. Don't propose a restart sequence; that is for our site procedure and shift supervisor.
prompts.caution: Never bypass interlocks or restart on AI advice; hydrogen leaks are invisible and ignite easily. The site's emergency and restart procedures govern.

prompts.title: Draft a maintenance procedure
prompts.task: Turn OEM manual sections into a site work instruction
prompts.prompt: You are a technical writer for an industrial gas plant. Draft a step-by-step work instruction for [TASK, e.g. replacing deionizer resin cartridges / swapping a hydrogen dryer filter / calibrating a catalytic H2 detector] on [EQUIPMENT]. Source material from the OEM manual and our site rules: [PASTE EXCERPTS]. Format: purpose and scope; required permits and isolations (LOTO, nitrogen purge and gas test to below [SITE LIMIT]); PPE and tools, including non-sparking tools and ATEX/IECEx-rated electronics in classified zones; numbered steps with hold points; acceptance checks; return to service; records to complete. Mark every place you had to fill a gap that wasn't in my source text with [VERIFY], and don't invent torque values, set points or limits.
prompts.caution: A draft for review. It must go through your site's management-of-change and procedure approval before anyone uses it.

prompts.title: Shift handover report
prompts.task: Turn shift notes into a clear handover and production summary
prompts.prompt: You are a shift lead at a green hydrogen production site. Turn my rough notes into a handover report for the next shift and the operations manager. Notes: [PASTE: production in kg H2, specific energy use in kWh/kg, power import and source, stacks online and offline, curtailment events, alarms, work permits still open, water treatment status, compressor and storage levels, trailer or pipeline offtake]. Structure: 1) safety and open permits first; 2) status of plant and equipment; 3) production and efficiency against target [TARGET]; 4) open issues with owner and next action; 5) items needing a supervisor decision. Keep it under one page, using plain sentences and a small table for the numbers. Flag any number in my notes that looks inconsistent (for example, kWh/kg outside [EXPECTED RANGE]).

prompts.title: Green certification data check
prompts.task: Check that operating records support RFNBO or 45V claims
prompts.prompt: Act as a compliance analyst familiar with the EU RFNBO delegated acts (additionality, temporal and geographical correlation), the US Section 45V clean hydrogen credit and its 45VH2-GREET emissions accounting, and voluntary schemes like CertifHy. Our plant is in [COUNTRY/REGION] and claims [SCHEME]. Power comes from [PPA DETAILS, grid share, EACs/RECs/GOs]. Our matching is [HOURLY/MONTHLY/ANNUAL]. Here's a sample of our records: [DESCRIBE OR PASTE]. List the data each requirement needs, which of my records match it, gaps or weak spots an auditor would likely question, and how phase-in dates affect us. Note where the rules are still changing or contested, and give the date of the regulatory text you're relying on so I can check it's still current.
prompts.caution: These rules have changed repeatedly; confirm with the scheme body, a certified auditor or tax counsel before submitting any claim.

prompts.title: Explaining safety to neighbours
prompts.task: Prepare plain-language answers for a community meeting
prompts.prompt: You are helping a hydrogen plant technician prepare for a community open house near our [SIZE, e.g. 20 MW] electrolysis site at [SETTING, e.g. an industrial park 500 m from homes]. We store [QUANTITY] kg of hydrogen at [PRESSURE] and use [WATER SOURCE AND VOLUME]. Write answers of 80 to 120 words each to the questions neighbours most often ask: explosion risk, the Hindenburg, water use, noise, truck traffic, what happens in a leak or fire, and whether it's really 'green'. Be honest about real hazards and how they're controlled under [APPLICABLE CODES, e.g. NFPA 2 / local permits]; don't promise zero risk. Then list three questions I should pass to the plant manager or the fire department instead of answering myself.
prompts.caution: Have communications and safety staff review answers; don't disclose security-sensitive layout or response details.

prompts.title: Planning work around renewable supply
prompts.task: Schedule maintenance windows against power forecasts and offtake
prompts.prompt: You are an operations planner for a renewable-powered electrolysis plant. I need to fit these jobs into the next [PERIOD]: [LIST TASKS with duration, crew, which stacks or systems go offline, and any dependencies]. Inputs: wind and solar forecast or expected low-generation windows [PASTE], power price or curtailment outlook [PASTE], offtake commitments [kg/day, storage buffer in kg], and crew availability [PASTE]. Suggest a schedule that keeps contracted offtake covered, does work in low-power windows where possible, and avoids running too many on/off cycles on stacks that are already degrading fast [LIST]. Output a day-by-day table plus the trade-offs you made, and the assumptions most likely to break the plan.
prompts.caution: Forecasts are uncertain; keep the final schedule under the operations manager's control and the plant's permit-to-work system.

prompts.title: Upskilling from another trade
prompts.task: Build a learning plan for moving into hydrogen work
prompts.prompt: Act as a training coordinator for hydrogen production technicians. I'm coming from [CURRENT BACKGROUND, e.g. refinery operator / industrial electrician / wind turbine technician] and I'm joining a [PEM/alkaline] electrolysis plant in [COUNTRY]. Make a 12-week study plan covering: electrochemistry of electrolysis and what drives efficiency; hydrogen properties and hazards (wide flammable range, low ignition energy, embrittlement, invisible flame); hazardous area classification (IEC 60079 / ATEX or NEC Class I); key codes such as NFPA 2, ISO 22734 and ASME B31.12; water treatment; compression and storage; and reading P&IDs and HAZOP studies. For each week list the topic, free or low-cost resources that actually exist (say if you're unsure a resource is current), and a practical self-check. End with the certifications or training courses most valued in [COUNTRY], noting which are emerging rather than established.
prompts.caution: Book learning does not replace site-specific induction and supervised competency sign-off.
